1.title: The Question on the Road
1.context: Baal-zebub was the god of Ekron, a Philistine city west of Israel. Ahaziah's embassy treats a foreign shrine as a medical oracle, and Elijah's intercepting question is about where Israel's king looks first in a crisis.
1.question: When something in your life breaks, where do you actually go first, and what does that say about what you trust?

1.title: Fire on the Hill
1.context: Twice a captain comes with a command in the king's name, and twice fire falls. The third captain comes on his knees and asks for mercy, and the story lets the contrast stand without commentary.
1.question: The first two captains and the third said nearly the same words. What made the difference in how they were received?

1.title: I Will Not Leave You
1.context: The sons of the prophets were members of prophetic communities found in several towns. Elisha refuses three chances to stay behind, using the same oath each time, and the journey becomes a farewell walked slowly on purpose.
1.question: Elisha knew the goodbye was coming and refused every early exit. Is there a goodbye in your life you are being asked to walk all the way through?

1.title: The Whirlwind
1.context: A double portion was the firstborn son's share of an inheritance, so Elisha asks to be treated as Elijah's heir in the work, not merely his attendant. Elijah leaves the answer with God: it depends on whether Elisha sees him taken.
1.question: Elisha asked for the heir's portion, responsibility and all. What would it mean for you to ask for more of the work, not less?

1.title: Salt in the Spring, Bears at Bethel
1.context: Bethel was the site of Jeroboam's golden calf shrine, a center of the rival worship. The severity of the scene there has troubled readers for centuries, and the text gives no explanation for it; it simply records it and moves on.
1.question: This chapter holds a spring healed and a road of judgment side by side. How do you hold both pictures of the same God together?

2.title: Seven Days Without Water
2.context: Moab's tribute in lambs and wool made it a wealthy sheep country under Israel's thumb. The southern route through Edom avoided Moab's strong northern border but crossed desert, and the plan failed on water before a battle was fought.
2.question: Three kings had armies, allies, and a route, and were defeated by thirst. Where has your best-laid plan run out of something basic?

2.title: Go to the Prophets of Your Father
2.context: Elisha's description, the man who poured water on Elijah's hands, marks him as Elijah's former attendant. His blunt answer to Jehoram shows that being used by God and being approved by God are different things in this book.
2.question: Elisha helped a king he openly disapproved of, for the sake of the one standing beside him. When have you been helped, or helped someone, only because of who else was in the room?

2.title: Dig This Valley Full of Ditches
2.context: The water arrived from the direction of Edom at the hour of the morning sacrifice, without wind or rain. To the Moabites at dawn it looked red, whether from the sun on red soil and rock or some other cause; the text says only how it seemed to them.
2.question: The instruction was to dig before there was any sign of water. What is the ditch you are being asked to dig on a promise alone?

2.title: The Sacrifice on the Wall
2.context: Child sacrifice was practiced among Israel's neighbors and is condemned throughout the Law. The great fury that follows Mesha's act is one of the most debated lines in the books of Kings; interpreters differ over whose fury it was and what it means, and the text does not explain it.
2.question: The campaign ends in a way nobody planned, at a wall, in silence from the narrator. How do you sit with a story God does not explain to you?

3.title: The Widow's Jar
3.context: Under the law, a creditor could take a debtor's children as servants for a debt. The miracle works through borrowed vessels and a shut door: the oil stops when the containers run out, not before.
3.question: The widow's part was gathering empty jars and pouring. What empty, ordinary thing in your life might God be asking you to bring?

3.title: A Room for the Prophet
3.context: Shunem lay in the Jezreel Valley on Elisha's regular circuit. The woman is called prominent or wealthy, and her contentment is the scene's quiet center: she asks for nothing even when a prophet offers to speak for her at court.
3.question: She said she had a home among her own people and asked for nothing. What would it look like to receive a gift you never dared to request?

3.title: Everything Is All Right
3.context: Her repeated answer, everything is all right, is spoken over a dead child, and readers have long debated whether it is faith, denial, or a refusal to waste the journey on anyone but the prophet himself. She reuses Elisha's own Jordan oath to hold him to the road.
3.question: She would not tell her grief to anyone who could not carry it to the source. Who gets to hear your real trouble, and why them?

3.title: Pick Up Your Son
3.context: The staff sent ahead accomplishes nothing, and the restoration comes only when Elisha himself arrives, prays, and gives his own warmth to the child. The scene echoes Elijah raising the widow's son at Zarephath in 1 Kings 17.
3.question: Gehazi's errand failed and the prophet's presence did not. Where have you sent a substitute when what was needed was your presence?

3.title: Death in the Pot, Bread for a Hundred
3.context: Wild gourds gathered in famine could be genuinely poisonous, and the flour remedy is given without explanation, like the salt at Jericho. The twenty loaves are firstfruits, the first ripe grain, brought to the man of God as an offering.
3.question: A hundred men ate from twenty loaves and had some left. Where have you seen a small offering outlast the arithmetic?

4.title: The Girl Who Spoke
4.context: Leprosy in the Bible covers a range of serious skin diseases. The girl serving Naaman's wife was war spoil from a raid, unnamed and enslaved, and her one sentence sets generals and kings in motion. Aram, modern Syria, was Israel's recurring enemy to the northeast.
4.question: The good news entered Naaman's house through its least powerful person. Whose small voice have you almost missed?

4.title: Wash and Be Cleansed
4.context: The Jordan was a muddy, unimpressive river beside the clear streams of Damascus, and Naaman's offense is the point: the healing required humbling himself at a servant's word in Israelite water. His own servants talk him down with a father's logic.
4.question: Naaman wanted a great ceremony and got a small obedience. What small, unimpressive instruction are you tempted to argue with?

4.title: Soil for an Altar
4.context: In the ancient world people commonly tied a god to its land, so Naaman asks for Israelite soil to stand on when he worships Israel's God at home. His question about bowing in Rimmon's temple is met without rebuke: go in peace.
4.question: Naaman's faith began with two loads of dirt and an honest confession about the compromises waiting at home. What does beginning honestly look like for you?

4.title: The Servant Who Ran After
4.context: Gehazi's lie borrows the Shunammite's words of truth, everything is all right, and invents two needy young prophets to make the fraud sound charitable. The leprosy that leaves the foreigner settles on the insider who tried to sell the gift.
4.question: Gehazi could not bear to watch a blessing given away free. Where are you tempted to put a price on what God gives without charge?

5.title: Chariots of Fire
5.context: The raiders' blindness and the feast that follows turn an enemy squad into guests, and the text says the raids into Israel stopped. The hills full of horses and chariots of fire answer Elisha's cry at the Jordan, when he saw Elijah taken.
5.question: The servant saw the same hills twice in one morning, empty and then full. What might you be seeing accurately but not completely?

5.title: The Siege and the Two Mothers
5.context: Siege famine prices in the text are deliberately grotesque: a donkey's head, eaten only in desperation, at eighty shekels, and dove's dung as fuel or food at five. The cannibalism of children was named in the covenant curses of Deuteronomy as the last horror of a besieged city.
5.question: The king wore sackcloth under his robes where no one could see. What hidden grief might the composed people around you be carrying?

5.title: A Price List for Tomorrow
5.context: A seah was roughly a third of a bushel, so Elisha's prices describe famine food becoming cheap overnight, flour for a shekel. The officer's answer, windows in heaven, is the voice of reasonable despair, and it is answered personally.
5.question: The prophecy was about tomorrow, spoken at the worst hour of the siege. What word are you being asked to believe before any evidence arrives?

5.title: The Lepers Find the Camp
5.context: Men with leprosy lived outside the city gate by law and custom. The sound that scattered the Arameans is attributed to the LORD directly. The lepers' conscience, today is a day of good news, turns hoarders into messengers in a single conversation.
5.question: The lepers nearly kept a deliverance to themselves because they had found it first. What good news are you sitting on that belongs to the city behind you?

5.title: Trampled at the Gate
5.context: The king's suspicion of a trap was reasonable generalship and wrong anyway. The officer dies at the gate he was assigned to manage, seeing the plenty he mocked arrive, in exact fulfillment of the word spoken over him.
5.question: The officer saw the promise kept and never tasted it. Is there a place where disbelief is costing you the meal itself, not just the hope of it?

6.title: The Woman at the King's Court
6.context: The woman's appeal follows the same pattern as the widow's: a prophet's instruction obeyed at cost, then a restoration that includes the income of the lost years. Gehazi, disgraced in the last episode he appeared in, is here found telling the king stories.
6.question: She returned to find her years away repaid, harvests included. What loss have you stopped expecting God to make whole?

6.title: The Prophet Weeps in Damascus
6.context: Elisha's answer to Ben-hadad is deliberately double: the illness itself need not kill him, and he will die. Hazael's protest, calling himself a mere dog, is the standard humility formula of a courtier, spoken hours before a regicide.
6.question: Elisha wept over evil that had not happened yet, done by the man standing in front of him. How do you treat people when you can see where their road leads?

6.title: Ahab's House in Jerusalem
6.context: Judah's Jehoram married Athaliah, Ahab's daughter, sealing the alliance Jehoshaphat had made between the two kingdoms. The lamp promised to David is the text's own explanation for why Judah survives kings like this.
6.question: The lamp burned for David's sake, not Judah's merit. Where is your life being carried by a promise made to someone before you?

7.title: Anointed in an Inner Room
7.context: Jehu's anointing fulfills the commission given to Elijah at Horeb years earlier, carried out by Elisha through a younger prophet. The commanders' garments spread on the steps are an improvised throne, and the ram's horn makes it public before Jehu can reconsider.
7.question: The commission waited a generation for its man and its hour. What unfinished assignment from an earlier season might be reaching its time?

7.title: Driving Like a Madman
7.context: Naboth's plot at Jezreel is where Ahab and Jezebel's crime met Elijah's oracle in 1 Kings 21. Jehu's question to Joram, how can there be peace, treats the queen mother's influence as the war itself, and the battle happens on the stolen field by design.
7.question: Jehu quoted an old oracle over a fresh corpse on the very ground it concerned. What unpaid account from the past is still shaping your present?

7.title: The Window at Jezreel
7.context: Jezebel's taunt names Zimri, who murdered his king and reigned seven days before dying in the fire he set himself. Her painted eyes at the window are a queen dressing for a confrontation she intends to win by presence, and the palace staff decide otherwise.
7.question: She faced the end dressed as a queen and quoting history. What are you relying on to face your hardest meeting, and is it holding?

8.title: Seventy Heads in Baskets
8.context: The guardians of Ahab's sons chose survival and were made the executioners of their own charges. Jehu's speech over the heaps assigns the act to prophecy, a framing the book itself will qualify within the same episode.
8.question: Jehu called the baskets the word of the LORD fulfilled. How do you tell the difference between obeying a hard word and using one?

8.title: Come and See My Zeal
8.context: The slaughter of Ahaziah's relatives at Beth-eked goes beyond the commission against Ahab's house, and the text records no word from God approving it. Jehonadab's Rechabites were a clan famous for strict vows, and his presence lends the purge a borrowed holiness.
8.question: Zeal can outrun its orders and call the overrun devotion. Where might your strongest conviction be exceeding what you were actually given to do?

8.title: The Double Verdict
8.context: Four generations of Jehu's sons did sit on Israel's throne, exactly as promised. Hosea, a later prophet, would speak of the blood of Jezreel being revisited on Jehu's house, a tension between the books that the text leaves standing.
8.question: The same reign is praised and faulted in consecutive verses. What would your own double verdict say, and which half do you listen to?

8.title: The Child in the Temple
8.context: Jehoiada's coup uses the temple guard rotation on the Sabbath, when double forces were present, and arms them with David's stored weapons. The Testimony given to the child king is the covenant document, the law itself placed in a seven-year-old's hands.
8.question: David's line survived because one woman hid a baby and one priest kept a plan for six years. Whose long faithfulness is your life quietly depending on?

9.title: The Chest with the Hole in Its Lid
9.context: Joash's chest is one of the Bible's earliest transparent offering boxes, counted jointly by royal scribe and high priest so neither office could skim alone. The verdict on Joash is tied to Jehoiada's lifetime, and the Chronicler's account, told later in this series, adds what happened after the priest died.
9.question: No accounting was required because the men acted with integrity. What would it take for your money handling to be described that way?

9.title: Fifty Horsemen Left
9.context: The unnamed deliverer of Jehoahaz's reign is never identified in the text; suggestions have included his son Jehoash's later victories. The Asherah pole still standing in Samaria marks how little the relief changed.
9.question: God listened to a king the book calls evil, because He saw the oppression. What does that tell you about praying from a bad record?

9.title: Strike the Ground
9.context: The east window faced Aram across the Jordan. Prophetic sign-acts like the arrows were understood as setting the pattern of the event, which is why a half-hearted striking draws anger: the king had performed his own limit.
9.question: The king struck three times and stopped, politely. Where are you rationing the very deliverance you asked for?

9.title: Three Victories, No More
9.context: Jehoash's three victories over Ben-hadad match the three strikes exactly, recovering the cities Hazael had taken from his father. The chapter's explanation for Israel's survival is the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, reaching back to Genesis.
9.question: Grace in this chapter is God remembering a promise centuries old. Which of His promises is carrying more of your life than your performance is?

10.title: The Thistle and the Cedar
10.context: Amaziah's restraint toward the assassins' sons quotes the law of Moses directly, a rare explicit legal citation in the kings' records. His Edom victory likely swelled him with captured wealth and confidence, and Beth-shemesh undid both in an afternoon.
10.question: Amaziah listened to the law about other men's sons but not to a fable about himself. Which kind of correction do you find easier to hear?

10.title: Prosperity Without Repentance
10.context: Jeroboam II's borders matched Solomon's at their widest, and archaeology remembers his era as Israel's most prosperous. The prophet Jonah son of Amittai appears here as a court voice of expansion; his own book, told at its place in this series, shows him very differently.
10.question: Israel's richest reign is summarized as evil in the sight of the LORD. What does your own most successful season look like under that measure?

10.title: Six Kings, Four by the Sword
10.context: Tiglath-pileser III rebuilt Assyria into an empire that deported conquered peoples as policy, scattering them to break national resistance. Galilee and Gilead, annexed first, were the territories across the Jordan and in the far north, the land's outer walls.
10.question: The deportation began at the edges years before the capital fell. What edges of your life get surrendered first when pressure comes?

10.title: The Foreign Altar
10.context: Ahaz's altar copy was diplomacy in architecture: worship remodeled on the conqueror's pattern as a loyalty display. The bronze altar he demoted dated to Solomon's dedication, and the Sea he took down had stood on twelve bronze oxen for three centuries.
10.question: Ahaz did not abolish worship; he redecorated it on a foreign pattern and kept the old altar for private use. What compromises in your life wear that same shape?

11.title: Three Years of Siege
11.context: Assyrian deportation settled conquered peoples across the empire to dissolve their identity, and Israel's exiles were placed in the far northeast, in Halah, Gozan, and the cities of the Medes. Hoshea's appeal to King So of Egypt bought him a prison cell instead of an army.
11.question: Hoshea's last bet was on Egypt, and it arrived as a cell. What unreliable rescue are you still counting on?

11.title: The Verdict, First Part
11.context: The sermon's charge that Israel did things secretly is pointed: the God being sinned against is the one who brought them out of Egypt. The warning through prophets and seers ran from Moses to the exile, the longest sustained patience in the story.
11.question: They pursued worthless idols and became worthless themselves, says the sermon. What pursuit is quietly deciding what you are becoming?

11.title: Removed from His Presence
11.context: The verdict names Judah in Israel's sentence while Judah still stands, a warning written into the record for the surviving kingdom. To this day refers to the exile community the book was written for, reading its own history as explanation.
11.question: The sermon was preserved as a gift to the survivors, not a gloat over the fallen. How do you read a hard record of the past as mercy?

11.title: New Tenants, Old Altars
11.context: The resettled peoples became known in later history as Samaritans, whose mixed worship and long feud with Judah run into the New Testament. The priest sent back to Bethel taught at the rival shrine itself, which may explain the mixture that resulted.
11.question: They worshiped the LORD but also served their own gods. What is your also, the loyalty that shares the altar?

12.title: The King Like David
12.context: Nehushtan, the bronze snake, dated to Moses in the wilderness, where it had been an instrument of healing. Hezekiah's destruction of a genuine relic, because it had become an idol, is the reform's boldest act: even true history can be smashed when it steals worship.
12.question: Hezekiah broke a real artifact from Moses' own hands because people were burning incense to it. What true and good thing in your life has started collecting the devotion owed to God?

12.title: The Speech at the Aqueduct
12.context: The Rabshakeh was a senior Assyrian officer, something like a chief of staff and spokesman. His argument used real theology, real economics, and the city's own doubts, which is what makes it the most dangerous speech in the book: almost every premise in it was true except the conclusion.
12.question: The people's answer to a brilliant, mocking argument was commanded silence. When is silence your strongest reply to a voice dismantling your trust?

12.title: The Letter Spread Before the LORD
12.context: Spreading the letter in the temple turns prayer into laying evidence before a judge. Hezekiah concedes the Assyrian record completely, the gods of the nations really were burned, and draws his line at the difference between wood and stone and the living God.
12.question: Hezekiah's prayer begins with who God is, not with the size of the army. How would your most urgent prayer change if it started there?

12.title: The Hook in the Nose
12.context: Assyrian kings carved reliefs of themselves leading captives by hooks and rings through the nose and lips; the oracle turns the empire's own imagery on its king. The defense of the city is grounded twice: for God's sake and for David's sake.
12.question: Sennacherib died worshiping in his god's temple, killed by his own sons. What do the things you trust do for you at the very end?

13.title: Fifteen Years Added
13.context: The stairway of Ahaz was likely a staircase whose steps served as a sundial, and the sign's direction mattered to Hezekiah: a shadow lengthening is ordinary, a shadow retreating is not. Isaiah's first word and its reversal both come through the same prophet within one courtyard crossing.
13.question: Hezekiah wept, prayed, and the sentence changed before the prophet left the courtyard. What have you stopped praying about because the answer seemed already settled?

13.title: Everything Shown to Babylon
13.context: Babylon in Hezekiah's day was a rising junior power resisting Assyria, so the envoys were potential allies, and the tour was partly alliance politics. The oracle's shock is that the distant junior partner, not the Assyrian at the gates, is named as the future plunderer.
13.question: Hezekiah called a sentence on his descendants good because it landed after his lifetime. What are you content to leave unsolved for the people coming after you?

13.title: The Son Who Undid It All
13.context: Manasseh came to the throne at twelve, likely under regents steeped in his grandfather Ahaz's ways. His Asherah pole stood in the temple itself, the house Solomon dedicated with a prayer that God would hear sinners and forgive, now furnished for the sins it anticipated forgiving.
13.question: One generation's reform became the next generation's rubble, from inside the same palace. What are you building that cannot survive being merely inherited?

13.title: The Measuring Line of Samaria
13.context: A measuring line and plumb line were builder's tools; used against Samaria and Ahab's house they had meant demolition measured out exactly. The book of Chronicles, later in this series, tells of Manasseh's capture and repentance, a part of his story Kings omits entirely.
13.question: Kings records no repentance for Manasseh at all. How do you handle knowing a person's worst record is not the whole of their story?

14.title: The Book Found in the House
14.context: The Book of the Law is generally understood to be Deuteronomy or its core, the covenant document Moses commanded to be kept beside the ark and read to the nation. It had been lost not by theft but by neglect, inside the building built to house it, across decades of idolatrous kings.
14.question: The book was in the house the whole time. What has been sitting unread in the middle of your life, waiting to be opened?

14.title: Huldah's Two Words
14.context: Huldah is consulted while Jeremiah is also active in Jerusalem, a sign of her standing. Her oracle is the reform's charter and its limit at once: the king's tears buy his own peace and not one day of delay for the sentence on the nation.
14.question: Josiah is heard because his heart was tender at bad news everyone else had ignored. What does a tender heart look like in you, and what hard word is it for?

14.title: The Great Purge
14.context: Josiah's campaign deliberately reverses the series: Bethel's altar and Jeroboam's sin, the founding breach of 1 Kings, are dismantled by a king of Judah acting as Israel's king in all but title. The spared tomb fulfills the man of God's own burial beside the prophet who had sheltered him.
14.question: The purge reached altars three hundred years old that every reformer before him had left standing. What old, respectable thing in your life is due for the Kidron treatment?

14.title: The Passover and the Nevertheless
14.context: No such Passover since the judges reaches back past the entire monarchy to the era of the deliverers. The Nevertheless that follows Josiah's superlative is the book's hardest hinge: personal faithfulness fully honored, national sentence fully unchanged.
14.question: Josiah's obedience changed his own end and nothing about the decree. How do you keep doing right when the outcome you want is already ruled out?

14.title: Megiddo
14.context: Pharaoh Neco was marching to prop up the last remnant of Assyria against Babylon, and Josiah's confrontation at Megiddo, the ancient chokepoint of the coastal highway, cost him his life at thirty-nine. Chronicles gives Neco a warning and Josiah a refusal, told when this series reaches it.
14.question: The reformer fell in a battle the book barely describes, at a crossroads far from home. What does his end say about the guarantees obedience does not come with?

15.title: Ten Thousand Captives
15.context: The first deportation deliberately removed the kingdom's skilled and leading classes, craftsmen and soldiers, leaving the poorest to work the land. Solomon's gold vessels, cut into pieces for transport, close a thread that began with the temple's dedication four centuries earlier.
15.question: The city was saved nine more years by a surrender that cost it everything portable. What have you preserved by giving up what you most wanted to keep?

15.title: The Last Thing Zedekiah Saw
15.context: Blinding a captured king and killing his sons before his eyes was Assyrian and Babylonian practice for rebel vassals, ending the dynasty in the man's last sight. The plains of Jericho, where the flight ended, are where Israel had crossed into the land in the book of Joshua.
15.question: The last king's story ends within sight of where the nation's story began. Where does your own long road seem to circle back to its start?

15.title: The Bronze Carried to Babylon
15.context: The temple burned a month after the city's fall, on a date later Jewish memory joined to the burning of the second temple as well. The bronze of Solomon's pillars and Sea was too heavy to move whole, so an age of craftsmanship left Jerusalem as scrap.
15.question: So Judah was taken into exile, away from its own land. What sentence in your life have you been reading as an ending that may only be a removal?

15.title: The Governor and the Flight
15.context: Gedaliah's grandfather Shaphan was the scribe who read the found Book to Josiah, so the governorship stayed in the family that had served the covenant. The flight to Egypt reverses the Exodus, the people running back to the house of slavery for safety.
15.question: Gedaliah offered peace on Babylon's terms and was murdered for it by his own side. When has doing the workable right thing cost you the support of your own people?

15.title: A Daily Portion
15.context: Evil-merodach, Amel-Marduk in Babylonian records, reigned briefly and is remembered in Babylonian sources as well. Jehoiachin's ration tablets, tablets recording oil rations for the captive king of Judah, were excavated in Babylon, a rare case of the exile's paperwork surviving outside the Bible.
15.question: The book ends with a dethroned king fed daily at his conqueror's table, alive and provided for, nothing explained. What small, unexplained mercy is your life currently running on?
